analysis.one_liner: Bans shipping companies and the Postal Service from charging higher rates or refusing service to Alaska, Hawaii, and U.S. territories.
analysis.headline: The bill has sat without any committee action since it was referred to two House committees on January 14, 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: Shipping companies and the U.S. Postal Service often charge more—or refuse to ship at all—to Alaska, Hawaii, Puerto Rico, Guam, and other noncontiguous U.S. areas. This bill would forbid charging a higher rate for shipping the same product to those areas than to the 48 contiguous states and D.C., and would ban excluding them from service. Items valued over $10,000 would be exempt.
analysis.who_benefits: Residents of Alaska, Hawaii, and U.S. territories including Puerto Rico, Guam, the Virgin Islands, American Samoa, and the Northern Mariana Islands would pay the same shipping rates as the rest of the country on most goods, and companies could no longer refuse to ship to them. Small businesses there that depend on receiving materials and selling products online would benefit too. The bill's sponsor is from Hawaii and its early cosponsors represent Guam, Puerto Rico, American Samoa, and the Northern Mariana Islands [S3].

how_it_helps.text: It bans charging higher rates to ship a product to a noncontiguous area than to a comparable location in the contiguous United States.
It prohibits shipping services from excluding noncontiguous areas from their policies or from shipping to their locations.
The rules apply to major private carriers and to the U.S. Postal Service, covering both consumer products and raw materials used in production.

analysis.who_pays: Private shipping companies and the Postal Service would give up surcharge revenue on noncontiguous shipments and could no longer decline those routes for covered goods. If they cannot charge more, they may shift some costs to customers everywhere or press for the $10,000 exemption to widen [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Parcel carriers and the Postal Service

drawbacks.text: The bill defines covered items narrowly (finished goods for end users and raw materials), and exempting anything valued over $10,000 leaves carriers free to keep surcharging higher-value shipments.
The text sets no enforcement mechanism or penalty beyond the prohibition itself, so its practical effect would depend on how regulators and courts apply it.
Carriers might respond by raising base rates nationally to offset the ban on noncontiguous surcharges, spreading costs to all shippers—though the bill itself does not state this.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit—ending surcharges and outright refusal to ship to Alaska, Hawaii, and the territories—addresses a real and costly burden on those communities, and it applies to a handful of large carriers rather than the whole economy. The drawbacks are enforcement difficulty and possible rate adjustments elsewhere, which honest supporters would acknowledge, and a $10,000 exemption that lets carriers keep pricing freely on higher-value goods. On balance the consumer benefit is real and the cost is likely modest, but the bill has drawn no committee action and faces long odds.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees the day it was introduced and has not moved since.

narrative.text: The House referred the bill to the Energy and Commerce and Oversight and Government Reform committees on January 14, 2025.
No committee hearing, markup, floor vote, or further action has occurred since the referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private shipping carriers and the Postal Service keep charging higher rates to noncontiguous areas, which remains the status quo. Shippers and consumers in the contiguous states are unaffected.

for.name: Rep. Ed Case
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and its only named sponsor.

for.name: Reps. Moylan, Hernandez, Radewagen, and King-Hinds
for.role: Original cosponsors (delegates and representatives from Guam, Puerto Rico, American Samoa, and the Northern Mariana Islands)
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors at introduction.

sides.party_line_note: The five cosponsors are mostly nonvoting-delegate-type members from affected territories and include both Democrats and Republicans, though no one from a contiguous state has joined.

industries.note: They could no longer charge surcharges on shipments to Alaska, Hawaii, or the territories or refuse those routes for most goods under $10,000. Residents there currently pay some of the nation's highest shipping rates, so this closes a premium-pricing channel.

The bill applies the same price and service rules to USPS, limiting its ability to set higher rates for noncontiguous destinations. It could compress revenue on those lanes but would guarantee universal service there.

industries.industry: Hawaii, Alaska, and territorial residents and small businesses
industries.note: Consumers and producers outside the contiguous states bear higher shipping costs on nearly everything they order. Equalized rates would lower everyday prices for them.

analysis.trajectory: Bills that sit without a hearing or markup in either referred committee this long rarely move. Unless a committee schedules action, it is likely to die quietly at the end of the 119th Congress.
